text: Two assassins shoot simultaneously; assassin A's bullet kills the victim while assassin B's bullet, though in flight, arrives too late. Why is this early-preemption case a problem for Lewis's simple counterfactual analysis of causation?
choices: Because the victim's death does not counterfactually depend on A's shot (had A not shot, B's bullet would still have killed the victim), yet A is the actual cause.
Because both shots overdetermine the death, so neither assassin can be assigned any causal responsibility at all.
Because the death counterfactually depends on B's shot rather than A's, wrongly identifying B as the cause.
Because counterfactual dependence is intransitive, so no causal chain from A to the death can be constructed.
explanation: In early preemption the effect fails to counterfactually depend on the actual cause: had A not fired, the preempted backup B would have produced the same effect, so the simple test wrongly denies that A caused the death. Option 1 describes symmetric overdetermination, a distinct case; the trouble here is precisely that there is a determinate actual cause (A) the counterfactual test misses.
